query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a controlled fraction of tungsten carbide (WC) particles into a high-entropy alloy (HEA) matrix via laser cladding will induce a self-adaptive, tribo-reactive nanocomposite layer during sliding that simultaneously lowers the friction coefficient and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional high-entropy alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi) produced without ceramic reinforcement and exhibiting baseline friction and wear performance.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled amount (on the order of 0.1–0.3 wt.% or optimized based on processing) of tungsten carbide particles into the HEA during laser cladding.
generation.conditions: The intervention is expected to be effective under sliding wear conditions spanning from room temperature up to approximately 800 °C, provided that the metallurgical bond and particle dispersion are maintained.
generation.structural_mediator: The uniformly distributed WC particles promote the formation of a dynamic, reactive tribo-layer that combines nanoscale oxides and/or WC-derived compounds at the worn surface.
generation.mechanism: During friction, the mechanical interaction and localized heating trigger tribocatalytic reactions at the WC/HEA interface, which lead to the in situ formation of a lubricious, nanocomposite layer that reduces both interfacial shear stress and material removal.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated HEA, the WC-reinforced HEA is predicted to achieve a significant drop (e.g., approximately 30–50% reduction) in the coefficient of friction and a reduction in the wear rate by nearly one order of magnitude over the tested temperature range.
generation.baseline: Untreated HEA showing higher friction coefficients and wear rates when subjected to identical test conditions.
generation.boundary: The improvement is contingent on maintaining a uniform dispersion and strong interfacial bonding of WC particles; deviations (e.g., particle agglomeration or interface defects) may impair the formation of the tribo-layer and limit the self-lubricating effect.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal WC content, long-term durability of the tribo-layer under cyclic loading, and potential effects of extreme thermal cycling remain to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples using identical laser cladding processing: one set with the optimized WC particle addition to the HEA and one set without (control). Subject both sets to ball-on-disk sliding wear tests at multiple temperatures from room temperature to 800 °C under identical load and speed conditions.
measurements: Steady-state coefficient of friction (COF) over sustained sliding cycles
Wear rate (volume loss per unit load per sliding distance)
Characterization of the worn surface (e.g., scanning electron microscopy for tribo-layer formation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the WC-reinforced HEA does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction (e.g., less than ~25% improvement over the control) in both friction coefficient and wear rate across the entire temperature range, or if the expected lubricious tribo-layer fails to form, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Recent studies have revealed that refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) based on refractory elements such as tungsten (W), molybdenum (Mo), niobium (Nb), and tantalum (Ta) exhibit superior high-temperature strength and good fatigue resistance, surpassing the currently used nickel-based superalloys [,]. However, RHEAs, such as the MoNbTaVW alloy [], typically have high densities and exhibit brittleness at room temperature, which limits their application scope. The addition of aluminum (Al), with its low density and large atomic radius, induces lattice distortions when forming solid solutions with refractory metals, reducing the system’s free energy, thereby enhancing solution strengthening effects. Therefore, Al is often added to RHEAs to reduce alloy density and improve specific strength. AbstractThe working environment of agricultural knives is bad, which makes the knives wear out easily. A wear resistant layer of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA) reinforced by tungsten carbide (WC) was prepared by laser cladding on one side of the cutting edge of a 65 Mn silage knife. Both the effects of WC addition on the microstructure and mechanical properties of AlCoCrFeNi (WC)x (x = 0, 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 in mass percentage) alloys were investigated. All experimental alloys displayed a crystalline structure of simple body centered cubic (BCC). The hardness of the cladding layer increases with the increase of WC content, and the hardness value enhances from 740 HV0.2 to 1060 HV0.2. A self-grinding edge was formed during working for the cladded knives. The cutting quality can be improved and the service life of agricultural knives can be increased meanwhile. The weight loss rate of untreated knives was about 2.64 times that of the cladded knives after a 76 h field experiment.Keywords: high entropy alloy, WC particles, self-grinding, microstructure, wear resistance
